narrative: During the 2000s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture continued to thrive as part of their rich identity and heritage. The natural hair movement, which originated in the United States during the 1960s but resurged in popularity in the 2000s, encouraged individuals with afro-textured hair to celebrate their natural beauty. Hairstyles such as Afros, cornrows, and box braids were (and continue to be) deeply rooted in African cultures and traditions, serving not only as a means of self-expression but also as a way to connect with one's heritage. Dreadlocks, Bantu knots, and protective hairstyles like locs also gained popularity during this time, allowing women to experiment with different styles while prioritizing hair health and durability. While the Jheri curl, popular in the 1980s and early 1990s, may have been on its way out by the 2000s, it is clear that Black and African women's hairstyles were (and continue to be) a vital aspect of their identity, culture, and sense of self.
